L159: cite144†Top L160: # Employment and Wages, Annual Averages 2025
L161: 
L162: The annual bulletin Employment and Wages contains employment and wage data from the cite145†Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) program aggregated by industry at the national, state, and county levels.

L186: 
L187: This web-only publication, Employment and Wages Online Annual Averages, is the successor to the annual print bulletin, Employment and Wages. The 2008 issue of the Employment and Wages bulletin was the final edition to be issued on paper in March 2010.
L188: The graphs that appeared in the print publication are no longer produced for the web-only publication. The newest improvement to the E&W comes in the form of interactive tables. The replacement tables include monthly employment and quarterly establishment and wage data for more series. The new tables include wage information for size data tables, which had not been available in the old tables.
L189: Questions regarding these data can be addressed to the QCEW program by calling (202) 691-6567 or by using any of the channels provided on the cite168†QCEW contact page .
L190: The quarterly County Employment and Wages news releases produced by the QCEW program as well as PDFs of all 2025 QCEW news releases can be found at the cite169†QCEW news release archive . County Employment and Wages news releases present employment and wages by county and are released within 6 months after the end of each referenced quarter. All data, at each level of geography, can be found at cite170†QCEW databases . All tables in this publication are available as PDFs on the above Web site.
L191: Questions regarding these data can be addressed to the QCEW program by calling (202) 691-6567 or by cite171†e-mail†data.bls.gov .
L192: cite172†Business Employment Dynamics (BED) news releases present gross job gains and losses and are released approximately 7 months after the reference quarter. Questions about BED data can be directed to the information line at (202) 691-6467 or by cite173†e-mail†data.bls.gov .
L193: Material in this publication is in the public domain and, with appropriate credit, may be reproduced without permission. This information is available to sensory-impaired individuals on request. Voice phone: (202) 691-5200; Federal Relay Service: 1 (800) 877-8339.

L201: ## Introduction
L202: Data contained in this publication represent the complete and final count of employment and wages for workers covered by state cite152†Unemployment Insurance (UI) laws and the cite175†Unemployment Compensation for Federal Employees†oui.doleta.gov (UCFE) program during 2025 for the 50 states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, and the U.S. Virgin Islands.
L203: Data are aggregated by geography at the county, metropolitan statistical area, combined statistical area, state, and national levels; by cite176†ownership for the private sector, as well as federal, state, or local government; and by cite177†industry†data.bls.gov as defined under the 2022 cite178†North American Industry Classification System (NAICS). County, state, and national level aggregates appear in the tables in this publication.
L204: These data are the product of a Federal-State cooperative program, the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW), also referenced as ES-202. State workforce agencies compile the data for both private- and public-sector workers from reports filed by employers each quarter and report it to the BLS.
L205: In 2025, BLS derived totals of 12.1 million establishments, 155.7 million employed, and $12.3 trillion in wages, from reports submitted to state workforce agencies by every employer covered by UI or by UCFE. Of these employers, those in private industry provided state workforce agencies with quarterly tax reports on monthly employment, quarterly total and taxable wages, and contributions for an average of 133.2 million wage and salary employees in approximately 11.8 million business establishments.
L206: Similar reports of monthly employment and quarterly wages were submitted by the federal government for 2.9 million civilian employees, by state governments for 4.9 million employees, and by local governments for 14.8 million employees. UI-covered employment reported by these sources constituted a virtual census (97.7 percent) of employees on nonfarm payrolls. The principal exclusions from UI and UCFE coverage are cited in the cite151†Characteristics and cite154†Employment sections of this publication.
L207: In this document, BLS presents cite96†data†data.bls.gov by cite176†ownership , cite177†industry†data.bls.gov , and cite179†area . These data include the average number of establishments, average annual employment, total wages, and annual and average weekly wages per employee. Additionally, BLS publishes national employment and wage totals for 11 supersectors, 21 sectors, and all 1,028 six-digit NAICS industries. County-level data include number of establishments, employment, and average weekly wage.
L208: Private-sector data are presented by cite179†area , from the total private ownership level to the six-digit NAICS industries. Private-sector data also are presented by national gross job gains and losses. State, local, and federal government data are detailed for selected industries.
L209: QCEW data for 2025 are classified according to the cite178†NAICS 2022 . QCEW has implemented cite178†NAICS 2022 with all data publication forward. For more information on the classification systems used by the QCEW program, please refer to the cite180†QCEW Industry Classification page .

L249: ## Characteristics of the data
L250: The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) compiled the data in this publication as part of the operations of its Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) program. Data are derived from the quarterly tax reports submitted to state workforce agencies by employers, subject to state UI laws and from federal agencies subject to the Unemployment Compensation for Federal Employees (UCFE) program.
L251: Each quarter, state agencies edit and process the data and send the information to the Bureau's national office in Washington, DC. The QCEW program provides the most complete set of monthly employment and quarterly wage data by six-digit industry at the national, state, combined metropolitan statistical area, metropolitan statistical area, and county levels.
L252: Data have broad economic significance for the evaluation of labor market trends and major industry developments, for data comparisons over time, and for interindustry comparisons.
L253: ### Unemployment insurance laws and coverage
L254: The employer reports that form the input to the QCEW are required by the Federal Unemployment Insurance Tax Act and its extensions. Initially, the Federal Unemployment Insurance Tax Act (1935) applied only to firms employing at least 8 persons for a minimum of 20 weeks in a calendar year and excluded certain categories of workers.
L255: Amendments to Title XV of the cite210†Social Security Act†www.ssa.gov established the UCFE program, which extended coverage to federal civilian employees effective January 1, 1955, and to workers in firms employing from four to seven workers effective January 1, 1956.
L256: Federal legislation, effective January 1, 1972, extended coverage of state UI systems to firms employing one worker or more in 28 states and expanded some of the statutory coverage provisions. (The remaining states previously had extended coverage to these small employers.) The 1972 legislation also brought coverage to employees of state hospitals, colleges, and universities.
L257: The Federal Unemployment Compensation Amendments of 1976 incorporated major changes in state UI laws effective January 1, 1978. Under the Federal Unemployment Tax Act (FUTA), states expanded coverage to include nearly all remaining state and local government employees, employees of nonprofit elementary and secondary schools, and certain domestic workers. Some states began implementing the amendments as early as 1976. The law also brought the U.S. Virgin Islands under the UI system.
L258: The 1976 amendments covered agricultural labor if performed for an employer who, in any calendar quarter in the current or preceding calendar year, paid cash remuneration of $20,000 or more to individuals employed in agricultural labor. The 1976 amendments also apply to employers who, on each of some 20 days in 20 different weeks during the current or preceding calendar year, employed at least 10 individuals in agricultural labor.
L259: Under a cite211†1981 United States Supreme Court ruling†tile.loc.gov , schools affiliated with religious organizations are not required to be covered under the UI system. Many of these schools, however, continue to cover their employees on a voluntary basis. Special provisions for railroad workers are made through the cite212†Railroad Unemployment Insurance Act†uscode.house.gov .
L260: Data for workers covered under the cite213†Railroad Retirement Board†www.rrb.gov and for those covered under the cite214†Unemployment Compensation for Ex-Servicemembers†oui.doleta.gov (UCX) program are excluded from the tables in this publication.
L261: In a number of states, certain types of nonprofit employers, such as religious organizations, are given a choice of coverage or exclusion. Under FUTA, all states must cover nonprofits that employ four or more workers. Some states have extended coverage to nonprofits employing one or more workers. Details on coverage laws are provided in cite215†Comparison of State Unemployment Insurance Laws†oui.doleta.gov , available on request from the Employment and Training Administration of the U.S.
L262: Department of Labor, cite216†www.doleta.gov†www.doleta.gov .
L263: While coverage is largely consistent, comparisons of data from one state to another should take into consideration the differences in UI laws among states. In addition, when UI-covered private-industry employment data are compared directly with other employment series, the coverage exclusions should be considered. See Table A under cite154†Employment (cite155†Coverage exclusions ) for details.
L264: For more detailed information about UI history in QCEW, please see the cite217†Federal Unemployment Insurance Employment Coverage Timeline page.
L265: ### Industrial classification
L266: 
L267: Employment and wage data developed in the QCEW program have been classified by industry since 1938. Data presented in this publication are classified in accordance with the cite178†2022 North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) . It is the product of a cooperative effort on the part of the statistical agencies of the United States, Canada, and Mexico.
L268: A six-digit NAICS industry code, specifically based on a description provided by the employer on a questionnaire, is assigned to each establishment by the state workforce agency. If a private or government employer conducts different activities at various establishments or installations, separate industrial codes are assigned, to the extent possible, to each establishment. For a searchable resource related to NAICS codes used by QCEW, see the BLS cite97†Industry Finder†data.bls.gov application.
L269: To ensure the highest possible quality of data, state workforce agencies verify and update, if necessary, the NAICS, location, and ownership classifications of virtually all establishments on a three-year cycle. Information for government units in the public administration sector, however, is verified less frequently. Each year, changes in establishment classification codes resulting from the verification process are introduced with the data reported for the first quarter.
L270: QCEW data for 2025 are classified according to the cite178†NAICS 2022 . QCEW has implemented cite178†NAICS 2022 with all data publication forward. For more information on the classification systems used by the QCEW program, please refer to the cite180†QCEW Industry Classification page.
L271: ### Employment
L272: 
L273: In general, QCEW monthly employment data represent the number of covered workers who worked during, or received pay for, the pay period that included the 12th day of the month. Virtually all workers are reported in the state in which their jobs are located.
L274: UI and UCFE coverage is broad and has been basically comparable from state to state since 1978, when the 1976 amendments to the cite218†Federal Unemployment Tax Act†uscode.house.gov became effective, expanding coverage to include most state and local government employees. In 2025, UI and UCFE programs covered 155.7 million jobs. The estimated 149.5 million workers in these jobs (after adjustment for multiple jobholders) represented 97.4 percent of civilian wage and salary employment.
L275: Covered workers received $12.3 trillion in pay, representing 94.6 percent of the wage and salary component of personal income, and 39.9 percent of the gross domestic product.
L276: Covered private-industry employment includes most corporate officials, executives, supervisory personnel, professionals, clerical workers, wage earners, piece-workers, and part-time workers. Persons on paid sick leave, paid holiday, paid vacation, and the like are also included. Persons on the payroll of more than one firm during the period are counted by each UI-subject employer, if they meet the employment definition noted previously.
L277: Workers are counted even though, in the latter months of the year, their wages may not be subject to UI tax.
L278: It excludes proprietors, the unincorporated self-employed, unpaid family members, and certain farm and domestic workers. The employment count also excludes workers who earned no wages during the entire applicable pay period because of work stoppages, temporary layoffs, illness, or unpaid vacations.
L279: Employment at all federal agencies for any given month is based on the number of persons who worked during, or received pay for, the pay period that included the 12th of the month. Employment data reported for federal civilian employees are a byproduct of the operations of state workforce agencies in administering the provisions of Title XV of the Social Security Act, the UCFE program.
L280: Federal employment data are based on reports of monthly employment and quarterly wages submitted each quarter to state agencies for all federal installations with employees covered by the Act, except for certain national security agencies, which are omitted for security reasons.

L307: #### Annual Average Employment
L308: 
L309: QCEW annual average employment is calculated by summing the twelve (12) months of employment (final) for a calendar year, and then dividing by 12. This is usually first published in June of the following year, with final annual average QCEW data available in September of that year. Please note that rounding may result in minor differences between hand calculations and the published annual average employment data from QCEW.
L310: 
L311: ### Wages
L312: #### Total wages
L313: Covered employers in most states report total compensation paid during the calendar quarter, regardless of when the services were performed. A few state laws, however, specify that wages be reported for, or be based on, the period during which services are performed, rather than for the period during which compensation is paid.
L314: Under most state laws or regulations, wages include bonuses, stock options, severance pay, the cash value of meals and lodging, tips and other gratuities, and, in some states' employer contributions to certain deferred compensation plans, such as 401(k) plans.
L315: #### Total wages exclusions
L316: 
L317: Covered employer contributions for old-age, survivors, and disability insurance; health insurance; UI; workers' compensation; and private pension and welfare funds are not reported as wages. Employee contributions for the same purposes, however, as well as money withheld for income taxes, union dues, and so forth are reported, even though they are deducted from the worker's gross pay.
L318: #### Average wages
L319: 
L320: Average annual wages per employee for any given industry are computed by dividing total annual wages by annual average employment. A further division by 52 yields average weekly wages per employee. Annual pay data only approximate annual earnings because an individual may not be employed by the same employer all year or may work for more than one employer at a time.
L321: Average weekly or annual pay is affected by the ratio of full-time to part-time workers, as well as by the numbers of individuals in high- and low-paying occupations. When comparing average pay levels among states and industries, data users should take these factors into consideration. For example, industries characterized by high proportions of part-time workers will show average weekly wage levels appreciably less than the weekly pay levels of regular full-time employees in these industries.
